intro_html:
Texas has no plug-in solar law, so a balcony panel that feeds a household circuit is a distributed generator like a rooftop array. In Houston that means CenterPoint Energy, which manages solar interconnections on its grid through an application and review process. It does not buy power or offer net metering; any credit for exports depends on the customer’s retail electricity provider. State rules require a utility to interconnect a facility with pre-certified equipment within four weeks of a completed application.

Texas does have a solar-access law, and it is narrower than it looks. Property Code §202.010 bars a property owners’ association, a term the chapter defines to include a condominium regime, from prohibiting a “solar energy device”, which the Tax Code defines broadly enough (“a system or series of mechanisms designed primarily to … produce electrical or mechanical power”) to take in a plug-in panel. But the association may still prohibit a device on property owned in common, or anywhere other than the roof or a fenced yard or patio the owner owns and maintains, and may require prior approval. Where a condo balcony is common property, the statute lets the association rule a panel out.

The statute protects property owners, not tenants. A renter needs the landlord’s permission and, for anything that feeds the home’s wiring, CenterPoint’s interconnection approval. balco.nyc’s savings figures below assume every kWh is used at home and none is sold.

faq: Does Texas's HOA solar law protect a balcony solar panel?

Only partly. Texas Property Code 202.010 stops a property owners' association, including a condominium association, from banning solar energy devices outright, but lets it prohibit one on commonly owned property or anywhere other than the roof or a fenced yard or patio the owner owns and maintains, and lets it require prior approval. It does not protect renters.
